A fragment is a small, broken-off, or incomplete piece of something that was — or is meant to be — a larger whole. The word has two closely connected uses, both built on the same central idea.

When something solid breaks apart, the individual pieces are called fragments. If a glass shatters on the floor, each piece is a fragment. If an archaeologist unearths part of an old clay pot, that piece is a pottery fragment. If a bone cracks and a sliver breaks away, that's a bone fragment.

In all these cases, the fragment was once part of something complete — and now it's separated, usually by force, accident, age, or decay.
Use 2: Something incomplete or cut off

"Fragment" is also used for non-physical things — thoughts, memories, conversations, writing — when you only have part of them, not the whole.

  • If you overhear only part of what two people are saying, you've caught a fragment of their conversation.
  • If you can only half-remember a dream, you have a fragment of a memory.
  • In grammar, if a group of words is missing what's needed to form a complete sentence (no subject, or no verb, or no complete thought), it's called a sentence fragment. For example: "Running through the park." — that's a fragment. You know something is happening, but the sentence feels cut off.

The common thread across both uses: a fragment is never the whole thing. It's always a piece — typically an incomplete, imperfect, or accidental piece, not a cleanly divided portion.

"Fragment" carries a quiet sense of incompleteness, loss, or damage. It suggests something once existed whole — and now it doesn't, or at least you don't have all of it.

This is why it feels different from the more neutral word "piece":

  • "I found a piece of the puzzle." → neutral; the piece is simply one of the parts, accounted for.
  • "I found a fragment of the puzzle." → implies the puzzle is damaged, scattered, or not fully intact.

This emotional weight makes "fragment" common in literary, poetic, or reflective writing: a fragment of hope, fragments of his old life, fragments of a broken world. Writers use it precisely because it suggests something is missing — something was once whole and no longer is.
How it differs from similar-looking words

These words are related but not the same:

Piece — The most neutral option. Any part of a whole, with no implication of damage or brokenness. You can slice a piece of cake intentionally. Fragments don't come from careful slicing.

Bit — Smaller and more informal. "A bit of advice." No sense of something having broken.

Shard — A sharp, jagged fragment from something brittle like glass or ceramic. A shard is always a fragment, but a fragment isn't always a shard. Shards specifically cut or pierce.

Scrap — A leftover piece, often seen as waste or of low value. A scrap of paper; scraps of food. More about being discarded than about being broken off.

Remnant — What remains after most of something is gone. The focus is on what's left behind at the end, not on the act of breaking. A remnant of a once-great civilization.

Chunk — A large, solid, rough piece. Almost the opposite of a fragment in size. Chunks are thick and substantial; fragments are small and broken.

Portion — A deliberate, intentional division. You cut something into portions on purpose. Fragments happen by breaking, not by planning.

The key distinction: a fragment implies that something broke, fell apart, or became incomplete — it was not cut or divided on purpose.

• Archaeology and history: a fragment of an ancient manuscript; pottery fragments; a fragment of Roman mosaic. Here it often means a piece of something old that survived while the rest was lost or destroyed.
  • Medicine and science: a bone fragment; a bullet fragment; a DNA fragment. A physical piece that has broken off within a living system or substance.
  • Grammar: a sentence fragment. A group of words presented as a sentence but missing something essential — typically a complete subject-verb structure.
  • Literature and everyday speech: fragments of memory; a fragment of the truth; fragments of a conversation. You have only part of what's needed to see the full picture.
  • Music and art: a fragment of a melody; a surviving fragment of the fresco. Part of a work that was lost, unfinished, or destroyed over time.
A picture to hold in your mind

Imagine a mirror that fell from a wall and shattered. Every piece lying on the floor is a fragment. Each one still catches light and reflects something — you can even see a partial image in each piece — but no single piece shows you the full picture. Together, they were a mirror. Separately, they are fragments.

That image captures the word precisely: a fragment is a broken-off piece that hints at a larger whole — but the whole is missing, damaged, or gone.
